findings.title: Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method
findings.body: The handler does not check `req.method` before processing. Combined with no CSRF protection and a single shared secret, this lets an attacker who learns the secret invoke the endpoint via GET (which Next.js does not JSON-parse by default, so `reqBody = z.parse(undefined)` will throw a 500), or submit via PUT/DELETE which could also expose side effects. The endpoint should explicitly require POST and reject other methods with 405.

findings.title: Unprotected JSON.parse after decrypt can crash the request
findings.body: `symmetricDecrypt` returns the raw decrypted bytes and the result is fed directly into `JSON.parse` with no try/catch. If the symmetric decrypt throws (bad key, tampered ciphertext, wrong padding) or the plaintext is not valid JSON, the handler crashes with an uncaught exception and returns a generic 500 instead of a 4xx. This also means the webhook secret check, user existence check, etc. cannot return a proper error. The decrypt and parse should be wrapped, and the result should be validated as an object before being assigned to `key`.

findings.title: findFirst-then-create is racy and can duplicate credentials
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ userId, appId })` followed by `update` or `create` with no transaction. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appId) can both observe no existing credential and both insert, leaving two `Credential` rows that downstream code (which does `findFirst` in e.g. office365video callback) cannot reliably deduplicate. Use `prisma.credential.upsert` with a unique compound key, or wrap the read/write in a transaction with appropriate isolation.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality
findings.body: The webhook secret is compared with `!==`. Although the secret is shared and not user-derived, attackers can in principle exploit timing differences to recover the secret byte by byte. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` against buffers of equal length (after a length check) to close this side channel.

findings.title: Credential type sourced from app metadata, not the request
findings.body: When creating a credential, the code uses `appMetadata.type` for `type` while the existing callbacks elsewhere in the codebase store values like `"google_calendar"`, `"hubspot_other_calendar"`, `"office365_video"`, etc. If `appStoreMetadata`'s `type` differs from the conventional string used elsewhere for the same app (or if the DB `app` row's slug does not match the metadata entry's slug), the new credential's `type` column will not match what CalendarService implementations later filter on, causing the freshly synced credential to be ignored.

findings.title: Minimum token schema is malformed and does not validate anything
findings.body: The schema is declared as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the literal string `"z.string()"` and Zod's `z.object` does not support arbitrary computed keys this way — it emits a warning at schema construction and the dynamic entries do not actually constrain any property. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: string }` with an additional unknown catch-all, so `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, `expires_in`, scopes, etc. are not enforced. The function should instead take the provider-specific `schema` argument when credential sharing is enabled (since the shared endpoint returns whatever format the host chose) or declare the real required fields.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: If the parsed response has no `refresh_token` field, the function sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Downstream code in e.g. GoogleCalendarService and office365calendar persists `key` (or uses the value) as an actual OAuth refresh token. Storing the literal string "refresh_token" and later sending it to Google's/MS's refresh endpoint will cause the next refresh to fail with `invalid_grant`, which the Google service interprets as "unrecoverable, mark credential invalid". Instead, the existing refresh token should be preserved when the response omits one.

findings.title: Outgoing credential-sync POST has no authentication
findings.body: When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, this function POSTs `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` to the configured endpoint with no auth header. The receiving endpoint cannot verify the request came from this Cal.com instance, and a network attacker (or anyone who knows the endpoint URL) can impersonate arbitrary Cal.com users to obtain refreshed tokens. The same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (and matching header name) that the incoming webhook requires should be sent on this outgoing request.

findings.title: Missing Content-Type header and inconsistent return shape break every integration
findings.body: Two issues: (1) The fetch sends a `URLSearchParams` body without `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, so the receiving endpoint that decodes the form will see empty fields. (2) The function returns either the original provider response (an axios/`googleapis` object with `.res.data`, `.access_token`, etc.) or a raw `fetch` `Response`. Every caller (googlecalendar, hubspot, larkcalendar, office365calendar, office365video, salesforce, webex, zoho-bigin, zohocrm, zoomvideo) immediately accesses fields like `res.data`, `response.json()`, `.accessToken`, `.access_token` etc. on the result. When credential sharing is enabled, those accesses will throw because the value is a `Response`, not the expected token object — so the feature breaks all integrations on the first refresh.

findings.title: Saves SafeParseReturnType envelope instead of parsed data into credential.key
findings.body: After the change, the code does `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ ..., data: { key } })`. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full Zod `SafeParseReturnType` (an object with `success`, `data`, and possibly `error`), not the parsed key. The credential row now stores `{ success: true, data: { ... } }` instead of the actual token object. The next time `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` runs it will throw and the credential will be unusable. Other integrations (`office365calendar`, `salesforce`, `zoomvideo`, `webex`) correctly do `...tokenResponse.data` or `...parsedToken.data` — only googlecalendar was updated incorrectly.

findings.title: Salesforce getClient refreshes the OAuth token on every instantiation
findings.body: `getClient` now unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint on every call, then writes the response to the DB. Previously Salesforce never did a refresh in this code path; every connection was constructed from the stored `credentialKey`. With the new code each `CalendarService` construction (and therefore each event create/update/getAvailability cycle that goes through the manager) makes an extra network round trip and a DB write. Add an expiry check before refreshing, matching the patterns used by googlecalendar / hubspot / webex.

findings.title: Non-OK responses are detected via statusText === "OK"
findings.body: The check `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` is fragile: HTTP status text is not guaranteed to be `"OK"` for 200 (it can be absent or empty in HTTP/2) and for many non-2xx responses `statusText` is still a non-empty string so the comparison misclassifies the response. Use `response.ok` (which checks 200–299) instead. With credential-sharing enabled the function will additionally return a `Response` rather than a parsed token, but the `statusText` check still has the bug described.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
findings.body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` evaluates to the encryption-key string when both env vars are set, or to `undefined`/`""` otherwise. Call sites use it in `if (!APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` (truthy check), which works in practice, but it is documented/used as a boolean flag. Coerce explicitly: `Boolean(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)` so the type matches usage and an empty-string secret cannot accidentally enable sharing.

findings.title: JSON.parse on req.query.state has no error handling
findings.body: `JSON.parse(req.query.state)` will throw a SyntaxError if the state parameter is not valid JSON, turning the OAuth `add` endpoint into a 500. This code path is exercised only on path renames in this PR, but the file was moved and is part of the changed set; a `try`/`catch` returning `undefined` (matching the early-return for non-string state) would be safer. Same issue in `decodeOAuthState.ts`.

findings.title: New webhook has no tests despite being the trust boundary for cross-instance credentials
findings.body: The endpoint accepts encrypted credentials that fully overwrite a user's third-party OAuth tokens (potentially including refresh tokens) for any app, gated only by a single shared secret. The PR description acknowledges no tests were added. At minimum: tests for wrong/missing secret (403), unknown user (404), unknown app (404), invalid encrypted payload (4xx, not 500), missing/short encryption key, and concurrent writes for the same (userId, appId) should exist before merge.
